title: Generics
objective: After this lesson you will be able to write generic functions and types, constrain type parameters with extends, read generic library signatures fluently, and recognize when generics add precision versus when they add ceremony.
why: Your utility belt keeps growing: firstElement for string arrays, firstElement for number arrays… or one function with any, which is no function at all. Generics solve the exact problem: one implementation, precise per-call types. Every serious library you use — React's useState, Array.map, Promise.all, Prisma's queries — is generic, so reading generics is a job requirement, and writing them is how your own abstractions stop leaking types.

blocks.text: Watch the three failed attempts at the same utility, and notice what each loses:
What we want is a *relationship*: the output's type should be the input's element type, whatever that is, decided per call. That's a job for a **type parameter**:

blocks.title: The mental model
blocks.text: A type parameter is a blank in a form the compiler fills per call by reading your arguments. You declare the shape of the relationship; inference supplies the specifics. It's function arguments, one level up.
Syntax, in all the places you'll meet it

You've already used all of this: `Promise<User>` is a generic type with one parameter; `useState<string>("hello")` is a generic function with an explicit argument; `Array<T>` and `Map<K, V>` are two-parameter generics. The syntax stops being scary the moment you see it's all the same one idea.
The killer generic ties *two* types into a relationship. The canonical example — a type-safe property accessor — uses two parameters, and inference wires them:

Read `K extends keyof T` as "K is one of T's property names" — a **constraint**. The call site can only pass keys the type actually has, and the return type `T[K]` becomes exactly the type of the property you named. One generic function, and every misuse is a compile error with the actual property names in the message. This signature is worth memorizing; you will use it for real.
Unconstrained type parameters accept anything, which means you can't do anything with them. Constraints narrow what's allowed so the body can act:

Note what the constraint bought in `logLength`: not just permission to call `.length`, but a *rejection of inputs that lack it*. Constraints tighten the contract in both directions — the body gains capabilities, the callers gain a check.
You now have everything needed to read the signatures you meet daily. Three famous ones, decoded:
Generics have a failure mode: generic-itis, where every function sprouts `<T>` regardless of need. The test is simple — **does the type parameter appear in a relationship that matters?**

blocks.title: Common mistake #5
blocks.text: Writing `fetchUser<T>(): Promise<T>` and having callers choose the type by wishful thinking. If the function determines the type, it must declare it or validate it — a caller-chosen T on unvalidated data is any with extra steps. Honest boundary: Promise<unknown> + a guard (Lesson 8).

items: Type parameters are per-call blanks the compiler fills from your arguments — one implementation, precise types everywhere
Constraints (T extends X) grant the body capabilities and reject unqualified inputs; defaults make parameters optional
The prop<T, K extends keyof T>(obj, key): T[K] signature ties arguments to results exactly — memorize it
React hooks, Array methods and Promise combinators are all this same machinery — you can now read them
If a type parameter appears only once with no relationship, delete it: unknown expresses that contract honestly

exercise.prompt: Write `groupBy<T, K extends string>(items: T[], keyOf: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]>` — a real utility (Lodash has one) that buckets items by a key the caller extracts. It must: (1) infer T from the array, (2) constrain K to the string the callback returns, (3) produce a Record whose keys are exactly the possible K values with T[] buckets, and (4) reject non-string keys at compile time. Then verify groupBy(courses, c => c.level) gives you Record<"Beginner"|"Intermediate"|"Advanced", Course[]> with full autocomplete on the result's keys.
hints: The output type Record<K, T[]> is the whole answer — declare it on the signature and let the body satisfy it.
For building the record at runtime, start from {} as Record<K, T[]> and accumulate: (acc[keyOf(item)] ??= []).push(item).
K extends string is the constraint that both lets you use K as a Record key and rejects number/symbol keyOf callbacks.
exercise.why: Every piece earns its place: T infers from the array so elements keep their type; K extends string both enables Record keys and documents that keyOf must return strings; and Record<K, T[]> ties the output's key set to what the callback can produce. The result has autocomplete for bucket names and compile-time rejection of typo'd access — a utility that's genuinely more than its JavaScript twin. The `{} as Record<K, T[]>` cast is the one accepted idiom here (an empty object is a degenerate record), noted precisely because the rest of the function stays cast-free.

quiz.q: first(["a", "b"]) with function first<T>(xs: T[]): T — what is the type of the result?
quiz.explain: Inference reads the argument: ["a","b"] is string[], so T binds to string and the call returns string. The type parameter resolves to a concrete type per call — that's the entire mechanism.

quiz.q: Why does `function logLength<T extends { length: number }>(x: T)` compile when it calls x.length?
options: The constraint proves every acceptable T has the property, so the body may use it
length is a special compiler-blessed method
T is really any under the hood
quiz.explain: Constraints are promises the compiler enforces: since only types with .length can be passed, calling .length inside is sound. And logLength(42) failing is the same contract working in the other direction.

quiz.q: prop<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] — what does prop(course, "minutes") return when course is { title: string; minutes: number }?
quiz.explain: K binds to the literal "minutes", and T[K] resolves to the type of that exact property — number. The result type follows the key you passed, checked against the real property names.

quiz.q: Which is a symptom of generic-itis?
options: A generic with two related type parameters
A type parameter that appears exactly once and adds no constraint or relationship
A generic method on an interface
quiz.explain: One appearance, no relationship = the parameter is decoration. The honest alternative is unknown (for inputs) or the concrete type (for outputs). Generics pay rent only when they connect two types or constrain inputs.

quiz.q: type EventMap = { login: User; error: Error } — which listener type is precisely typed for bus.on("login", handler)?
options: handler: (payload: User) => void — payload type follows the key literal
quiz.explain: on<K extends keyof EventMap>(key: K, handler: (payload: EventMap[K]) => void) makes the payload follow the key: "login" → User, "error" → Error, wrong payloads rejected at compile time. This indexed-access pattern is the typed event-emitter idiom.

summary: Generics are per-call blanks: one implementation with type parameters that inference fills from your arguments. Constraints grant body capabilities and reject unqualified inputs; defaults make parameters optional; and the keyof/indexed-access combination ties argument choices to result types exactly. Read useState, map and Promise.all as the same machinery — and delete type parameters that appear once with no relationship.
next: The type system ships a toolbox of prebuilt generic transformations — Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType and friends. Lesson 7 makes them automatic refactoring tools instead of mysterious incantations.
